She set the catalogue on the sideboard, where the last three lay unopened, and took her coat from the hook. Outside the frost had gone soft and the lane smelled of wet leaves. text: In the hour after sunset, on the night of the first frost, Maelys climbed the lighthouse stair with a can of oil and her grandfather's brass key. The rail burned cold under her palm, and rime had already feathered the gallery glass. She trimmed the wick, wound the clockwork, and watched the great lens begin its slow turn, throwing a white arm across the darkening water. She had sorted mail in this village for thirty-one years and never once received a parcel herself. text: In the grey hour just after sunrise, with the spring flood running brown and loud over the ford, Wanjiru poled her raft toward the far bank where a single traveller stood waiting beside a mule. The river had swallowed the stepping stones a week ago, and drowned willows combed the current on either side. She kept her eyes on the rope and the water until the raft nudged the gravel. Then the traveller pushed back his hood and laughed, and she knew the laugh before the face: her brother Kamau, eleven years gone to the copper mines, grey at the temples now, holding out the wooden whistle she had carved him as a child. She shipped the pole and let the river wait while she held him.

text: In the hour before midnight, in the week the leaves came down, the circus struck its tent for the last time that season, and Nilufar stood apart from the lantern light with one small trunk at her feet. Wet poplar leaves plastered the wagon roofs and stuck to the horses' flanks. For nineteen years she had walked the high wire above these same faces; tonight her knee had trembled, and only she had noticed. She found the apprentice, Sabir, coiling rope, and pressed her rosined slippers into his hands without a word. Then the wagons rolled east toward winter quarters, bells clinking, and she took the western road alone, not looking back until the last lantern was a seed of light among the bare trees.

The air tasted of iron; her braids lifted from her shoulders. She had the grey one by the halter when the hair on her arms stood up, and without thinking she dropped the rope and threw herself flat among the ichu grass. The sky split. White fire struck the cairn ten paces off, and stones flew like startled birds. When she could hear again, the kettle was shrieking indoors, both llamas were staring at her, and she lay laughing into the wet earth.

text: When the street lamps came on along Adum Road, blurred by the first harmattan dust of the year, Kwabena set down his shears and did not light the shop lamp. His apprentice, Efua, was folding the chief's funeral cloth, the commission everyone said only Kwabena's hands could cut. He watched her for a while. Then he told her what he had told no one in forty years: that the pattern which made his name had been drawn by Yaw Mensah, the journeyman he dismissed for arguing, and that he had traced it the night Yaw left. Efua said nothing. She went on folding. Kwabena took his brass nameplate from the window, turned it face down among the pins, and felt lighter than the dust.

text: The tide did not cross its eleven paces. It sent one brown thread of water along the foot of the hurdles and up the alder's narrow edge, against the grain, as far as the bite. There it stopped and dried to a white crust the shape of her teeth. This is the Zennaquil, the tide's countersign, given only on marks it did not see made. Having signed, the water laid the eel-bone pin flat across the gap between the two withies, like a sill, and drew back to the first hurdle. But a Zennaquil is a thing entered in the weir, and Ysolde Kvarn had not notched it. The heron stepped to the fifth post. She tasted salt and counted the six posts left.

Ysolde clicked: two of eleven, received by her own tally, under water, where she cannot read it.

text: At the third dawn the Enghazul shifted a mouth's width and pressed its new ring to the alder beside the old one. But the old one was still wet. The alder's face below the waterline is the Lumetharc: neither bark nor pale, it keeps not what was caught or lost but what is still going on, and any mark there is entered afresh each dawn it stays wet. So yesterday's Uthmagrel paid again. Ysolde Kvarn clicked twice: four of eleven on the third day. Hands in her coat, she ran the sum forward on her teeth. Seven tomorrow. Eleven the dawn after, exactly as the pin runs out. And the dawn after that, with four rings still wet, the tally at Threnby Sluice would begin owing rent to a fish.

text: At the fourth dawn the Enghazul shifted to the pin's last mouth-width and pressed a third ring to the Lumetharc. The two old rings paid again. Ysolde Kvarn clicked three times: seven of eleven. Then something went out by the open gap in the first hurdle, where the pin-sill had been. It was one of the three lampreys taken while she was at Ochrevant, and never notched. A catch that leaves a weir before the keeper cuts it is a Navrithel: it cannot go on the pale face, since nothing uncounted can be lost. The heron should have stepped back to the fourth post. It leaned, the iron ring rang once against the wood, and it stayed. The Chelvarig now said five for four.

text: At the seventh dawn the alder paid four more and stood at nine of eleven, its pale face a hand above the water. Ysolde Kvarn unclicked four times. Then she did the one sum left to her. The Chelvarig said five for four, and a post overstated in the second tally is an Achtemoul: a charge already stood for, spendable once, with any creditor. She turned her head toward the first hurdle and clicked forward, once. The tide did not cross its eleven paces. Round 4: the bell stopped with her still at the window; the two abandoned pins lay in the shutter's groove so it could not fall; the ledger has no column for money returning, and the pins are not hers since she did not take them; the clerk fetched the Vellocht (whalebone tongs for sums that belong to nobody) and stood holding one pin in the air as the tide turned in the culvert; she offered him the wrong side of the debt-stick. Round 8: at the eighth mile she passed the Haugrenth (a tarred gauge-post hung with iron rings by which the tide-office reads the water's height; ten rings are numbered, the eleventh and topmost is bare and had never been wet); she passed at the count of four without looking round and heard the eleventh ring knock once, wet; at Threnby Sluice she took her place at the alder tally, hands still in coat; the tide stopped eleven paces off at the weir's first hurdle and set the pin upright between two withies, in the gap where a lamprey would go; the heron moved from the third post to the fourth. text: After the half hour the dog did not bark again. She took the socks from the second chair, turned them over once, and laid them back as they had been. The turf burned down slowly and she let it. Near eleven she thought she heard a step on the road, and this time she stood, and went as far as the door, and stood with her fingers on the latch without lifting it. The step, if it was a step, did not come on. She listened until the cold of the iron had gone into her hand. Then she went back, trimmed nothing, moved nothing, and sat down in her own chair beside the other. The lamp burned low in the window. The clock gathered itself and struck eleven, and she counted every stroke.

text: The half hour struck once and the sound went out of the room slowly. She hung the kettle over the fire after all, and when it began to murmur she warmed the chipped cup with a little of the water and emptied it into the basin, as if tea were only a minute off. The lamp burned steadily in the window. She stood beside it and looked up the road, white to the turn of the hill, and saw that the frost had filled in the day's cart tracks. No one had come down it. She lifted the kettle off before it could boil dry again, set it on the hearthstone, and went back to her chair. Her hand found the blanket. Toward one the turf settled, and she sat and listened to it.

A draught came under the door and bent the lamp flame in the window, then let it stand. She rose and laid her shawl along the foot of the door, and went back without it. The turf had burned to a steady glow. She sat with her hand on the blanket, a little colder now, and listened to the clock going on toward the half hour.

text: The half hour struck and the sound went out of the room slowly. Without the shawl the cold found her shoulders, and she did not go to the press for another. She drew the second chair a hand's breadth nearer the hearth, so the blanket and what lay under it would keep the heat. The lamp burned steadily in the window now that the draught was stopped. She went to it and looked out: the frost had closed the pane entirely, and she did not clear it. A light that could be seen from the road did not need her to see the road. She touched the cup's handle, still turned to the door, and sat down again, her hand on the blanket, while the clock went on toward two.

text: Two struck, and she counted both, because there were so few. The turf had fallen in on itself and she built it up again with two more, not sparing them now. The kettle on the hearthstone had gone cold; she carried it back to the crook and let it hang there, low, where it would warm without boiling. The oil in the lamp was down to a finger's depth, and she filled it from the can without putting out the flame, her hand steady. Somewhere up the hill a cock crowed, hours wrong, and was quiet. She lifted the corner of the blanket, found the socks warm, and laid it down again. Then she sat, her hand where it had been, and the clock went on toward the half hour.

text: The half hour struck its one note. She had not slept, though her chin had gone down twice. The kettle was low; she topped it from the bucket and hung it back on the crook, and the murmur stopped and by and by began again. The cup on the hearthstone was almost too warm to hold, so she drew it back a hand's breadth, the handle still toward the door. She laid one turf on, no more. At the window the frost had thickened, and the lamp made a small gold room of the sill. Somewhere up the hill a cart wheel, or the thought of one, turned over once and was gone. She sat down again, straight-backed, her hand on the warm blanket, and listened toward four.

text: Four struck, and she counted the strokes on her fingers against the blanket. The turf had caught and was burning evenly. She took the cup from the hearthstone, held it a moment in both hands for the warmth, and set it back with its handle toward the door. The kettle murmured. She went to the window; the frost was whole across the glass, and behind it the lamp burned without a waver. Out in the yard the gate gave one small creak on its hinge and was still, and she stood with her head turned until she was sure it was only the cold working in the iron. Then she came back and sat with her hand on the blanket as the clock went on toward the half hour.

text: The half hour struck its single note. She had let her head rest a moment against the back of the chair, and the sound brought it up again. The kettle had sunk to a whisper; she swung the crook a little out from the heat and let it hang. The cup on the hearthstone was warm through, its handle toward the door. She lifted the corner of the blanket, felt the socks beneath, and smoothed it down. At the window the frost had not thinned, but the glass above it was no longer quite black, only a deep slate, and the lamp looked smaller against it. Somewhere up the hill a bucket rang once on stone. She sat again, hand on the blanket, and listened toward five.

text: Five struck, and she counted the strokes aloud, softly, as she had counted nine. The slate above the frost had gone to grey, and the lamp in the window no longer threw its gold room on the sill; she did not lower the wick. She swung the crook back over the heat, and the kettle found its murmur again. She laid on a turf and turned the cup on the hearthstone so its other side took the warmth, handle still toward the door. Up the hill a door opened and shut, and a man called once to a dog. She took her shawl up from the foot of the door, shook the cold from it, and laid it down again. Then she sat, hand on the blanket, as the clock went on toward the half hour.

text: Restoring a dead electrotyping bath, as practised at the mission press-works, Tharangambadi, Coromandel coast, 1898. Fault: no copper shell forms on the cathode after six hours. 1. Lift the wax mould by its wire and inspect the plumbago coat; bare patches will not take. Re-brush with a camel-hair pencil until the face shines like a stove. 2. Check the hook where wire meets rod; verdigris there starves the whole basin. Scour bright with pumice. 3. Float the scale in the liquor. If it rides high, the sulphate is spent; dissolve fresh crystals in a pipe-fed jar and add slowly. 4. Rock the lever of the agitator twenty strokes. 5. Rehang the mould facing the anode plate, one hand's breadth apart. Do not hurry copper; a shell grown overnight prints ten thousand hymns.

text: Servicing the Single-Line Token Instrument, Kadugannawa cabin, Ceylon Government Railway, 1927. 1. Before opening the case, telephone the cabin at Balana and obtain the stationmaster's line-clear; record it. 2. If the token will not withdraw, do not force the slide. Check the galvanometer: no deflection means a dead battery or a broken line wire on the incline. 3. Test each Leclanché cell; replace any below one volt. 4. Clean the commutator contacts with spirit, never emery. 5. If the plunger sticks, suspect damp; dry the coil over the signal stove, then varnish. 6. Count the tokens in both magazines; the sum must be the number engraved on the brass plate. 7. Lock the case, seal it, and sign the fault register. Never release a train on a verbal promise.

text: Atuona, Hiva Oa, 14 March 1903. Monsieur Vasseur, I write to beg your patience, not your pardon. Of the six dozen dry plates you advanced me on credit, forty-one are spoiled: the damp of this valley crept into the box and bloomed the gelatine like mould on bread. The remaining thirty-one I have exposed, mostly portraits of the copra planters and one wedding at the mission, and I am owed in turn by every sitter. I can send you eighty francs by the next schooner, and my tripod as surety if you insist, though without it I cannot earn the rest. Grant me until the July steamer and you shall have the whole sum with interest. Your obedient debtor, Théodore Malzac.
